subject: Civil Engineering
title: Change Orders
description: Learn Change Orders in one minute.

hook.text: The owner wants an extra floor. The soil is worse than expected. Plans must change.

buildup.text: A change order modifies the original contract — adding scope, time, or cost.

discovery.text: Each change order must be priced, negotiated, and approved before the work proceeds.

twist.text: Contractors sometimes bid low, expecting to profit from change orders — a common industry tactic.

climax.text: Boston's Big Dig had over 7,000 change orders — costs ballooned from $2.8B to $14.6B.

punchline.text: Every change costs more than the original plan. The cheapest change is the one you avoid.

quiz.question: Why did Boston's Big Dig cost five times its original estimate?
options: Inflation raised material costs dramatically during construction
Over 7,000 change orders accumulated, each adding scope, time, and cost
The project was redesigned from scratch three times

details.summary: Change orders are formal modifications to the original construction contract that adjust scope, cost, time, or all three. They arise from design errors, owner-requested changes, unforeseen site conditions, or code revisions.
details.whyItMatters: Change orders are the most common source of construction disputes and cost overruns. Managing them effectively requires clear documentation, fair pricing, and prompt processing to avoid delays.
takeaways: Change orders modify the original contract scope, cost, and schedule
Design errors and omissions are the largest source of change orders
Prompt processing prevents delays and disputes from accumulating

faq.question: How are change order costs determined fairly?
faq.answer: Costs are typically based on actual labor hours at agreed rates, material costs with receipts, equipment usage at established rates, subcontractor quotes, and agreed markups for overhead and profit. Unit prices from the original contract apply when available.

faq.question: How can change orders be minimized on a construction project?
faq.answer: Complete and coordinated design documents reduce design-related changes. Thorough site investigation reduces unforeseen condition claims. Clear scope definition in the contract prevents interpretation disputes. Owner decision-making discipline prevents late changes.
